_readme: Curated static reference layer for the map. Every fact carries its source URL, the source's own date, and when/how it was read. Coordinates are NOT taken from the cited sources: they were entered from general public geography and are approximate (see precision). Facts were read via page-fetch summaries on 2026-10-09 and are NOT human-reviewed (verified_by says so). A relation or fact missing here means 'not supported by a source I could read', not 'does not exist'. Static background only: nothing here states current operating status. `aliases` are names used ONLY to detect an asset explicitly named in an item's text.

assets.name: Strait of Hormuz

facts.claim: Oil flow through the strait averaged about 20 million barrels/day in 2024 (about 20% of global petroleum liquids consumption); flows in 1Q25 were roughly flat vs 2024.
facts.source_title: EIA Today in Energy article on the Strait of Hormuz (published 2025-06-16; title not captured)

facts.claim: About one-fifth of global LNG trade transited the strait in 2024, mainly from Qatar (share of global trade, not a volume).
Saudi Arabia's crude and condensate exports were 38% of Hormuz crude flows (5.5 million b/d) in 2024; UAE and Kuwait volumes were lowered by OPEC+ cuts.

assets.caveat: Historical flow context, not current throughput. Does not say whether the strait is open or restricted today.

assets.name: Saudi East-West crude pipeline (Abqaiq → Yanbu)
assets.line_note: Schematic straight line between the two endpoints named by EIA; NOT the real route.

facts.claim: Stated capacity 5 million b/d (temporarily expanded to 7.0 million b/d in 2019); runs from the Abqaiq processing center near the Persian Gulf to Yanbu on the Red Sea. EIA labels it an Aramco pipeline.
EIA estimates about 2.6 million b/d of Saudi + UAE pipeline capacity could be available to bypass Hormuz in a disruption; these pipelines often do not run at full capacity.

assets.caveat: Capacity is not current utilisation or spare capacity.

assets.name: Abqaiq processing center

facts.claim: Named by EIA as the starting point of the East-West crude pipeline.

assets.caveat: Only its role as a pipeline start is sourced here; no throughput or status claims.

assets.name: Yanbu (Red Sea port)

facts.claim: Named by EIA as the Red Sea end of the East-West crude pipeline.

assets.caveat: Only its role as a pipeline endpoint is sourced here.

assets.name: Fujairah oil export terminal

facts.claim: The Abu Dhabi Crude Oil Pipeline (about 406 km) carries crude from an ADNOC Onshore collection center in Abu Dhabi to the Fujairah export terminal, giving access to the Arabian Sea; the pipeline entity is wholly owned by ADNOC.
Stated UAE pipeline capacity 1.8 million b/d, linking onshore fields to Fujairah on the Gulf of Oman.

assets.caveat: The pipeline's origin point is not specified in the sources read, so no line is drawn. ADNOC's page gives no capacity figure; the capacity above is EIA's.

assets.name: Jask export terminal (Goreh–Jask pipeline)

facts.claim: Iran's Goreh–Jask pipeline has effective capacity of around 300,000 b/d and connects to the Jask terminal on the Gulf of Oman; EIA does not state the pipeline's start point.

assets.caveat: Effective capacity as characterised by EIA in 2025; not current throughput.

assets.name: Bab el-Mandeb Strait

facts.claim: Combined oil shipments via the Suez Canal, SUMED pipeline and Bab el-Mandeb were about 12% of total seaborne-traded oil in 1H 2023. The article gives no separate volume for Bab el-Mandeb.
facts.source_title: EIA Today in Energy: Red Sea chokepoints are critical for international oil and natural gas flows

assets.caveat: Dated 2023 and combined with Suez/SUMED; says nothing about current traffic.

facts.claim: The SUMED pipeline connects the Red Sea with the Mediterranean through Egypt; stated capacity 2.5 million b/d.
facts.source_title: EIA Today in Energy (Red Sea chokepoints)

facts.claim: Combined Suez Canal LNG flows peaked at 4.5 Bcf/d in 2021 and 2022 and were 4.1 Bcf/d in 1H 2023.

assets.name: Ras Laffan Industrial City (Qatar LNG hub)

facts.claim: QatarEnergy describes Ras Laffan as its onshore base for processing North Field gas, about 80 km north of Doha on the Persian Gulf coast; Ras Laffan Port is described as owned and operated by QatarEnergy with six LNG berths.
facts.source_title: QatarEnergy — Industrial Cities / Ports Information (read through a search-result summary, not the full page)

facts.claim: QatarEnergy LNG's corporate-structure page lists shareholders and capacities for each venture (e.g. N(2) trains 4–5 at 7.8 MTPA each; NFE ventures marked under construction). It does not itself state that the ventures are at Ras Laffan.

assets.caveat: Third-party reporting (not cited here) describes damage to Ras Laffan in March 2026; current operating status was not checked. This entry is background only.

relations.detail: Abu Dhabi Crude Oil Pipeline (the pipeline entity feeding Fujairah) is wholly owned by ADNOC.
EIA labels the East-West crude pipeline as Aramco's. Ownership/operatorship was not checked against Aramco documents.
Ras Laffan Port described as owned and operated by QatarEnergy.

Per QatarEnergy LNG's table: 30% of N(2) Train 4; 18.3% of N(2) Train 5; 30% of S(3). The table does not state the ventures' location; the Ras Laffan link is inferred from the other QatarEnergy page and is not a sourced statement.
relations.verified_by: agent (page-fetch summary); not human-reviewed; location link inferred

relations.detail: Per the same table: 30% of N(4) Train 7; 25% of NFE(2) (under construction). Location link inferred as above.
relations.verified_by: agent (page-fetch summary); not human-reviewed; location link inferred
